📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

For the third time in a row, Google Cloud is recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Application Development Platforms, positioned highest overall on the Ability to Execute axis.1.

According to recent reports, these days, it’s very clear to us that organizations are looking for AI to handle actual day-to-day work, stay strictly within compliance guardrails, and deliver measurable ROI. In the last year, nearly 500 Google Cloud customers each processed more than one trillion tokens. And a lot of that volume came from heavily regulated sectors like global banking, healthcare, and telecommunications.

Our customers choose Gemini because it delivers an open enterprise platform built for this level of production scale, by:.

Unifying the agent experience across everyday workflows.

Providing unrestricted model choice without vendor lock-in.

Practicing cost discipline before bills spiral, not after.

Governing agents through a single, centralized control plane.

In October, we announced a unified Gemini experience. The same Gemini you collaborate with every day is now your enterprise agent to get real work done. Instead of navigating disconnected developer consoles, consumer tools, and workplace add-ons, Gemini meets work wherever it already happens – collaborating natively inside surfaces like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, internal chats, web, and mobile.

According to recent reports, you give Gemini high-level business objectives rather than step-by-step instructions, and it orchestrates the necessary tools, context, and coworker agents to deliver a finished result. As employees engage it, the agent retains persistent memory, understands your specific business language, and respects enterprise permissions across every device. When a team automates a complex procedure, they can package it into a shared skill, turning one group’s procedural knowledge into a capability anyone across the organization can use.

“When you can use natural language, anyone from HR to sales can turn their unique business experience into a custom AI agent in minutes. In two months, we created over 600 agents. The majority were built by our frontline business teams right inside Gemini, leaving our developers to focus on more complex challenges.” – Robert Howes, Chief Technology Officer, Dojo.

Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading frontier model families, from Google, Anthropic and OpenAI, on a unified enterprise platform – and across every surface, from developer tooling in Antigravity to everyday productivity in Gemini for web, mobile, and desktop. Through the model garden, organizations can access over 200 models, drawing down existing cloud commitments on a single invoice without having to negotiate separate contracts.

Sources indicate that at the same time, we are deeply proud of the pace of innovation coming out of Google DeepMind. Over the past month alone, we’ve rolled out a full generation of specialized models: Gemini 4 Argon for strong performance across complex software engineering, law, finance, and cyber defense; Gemini 4 Carbon for frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows; and now Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence with speed and efficiency to everyday coding and agentic execution.

By treating models as a diversified portfolio, we give our customers the freedom to optimize for speed, precision, and cost across every task. For PayPal, this flexibility is central to their strategy:.

Sources indicate that “We built a unified LLM stack. That meant we ran our open source models on top of our inferencing stack on GKE, and we ran our close-sourced models on top of the Gemini platform. Developers get choice – Claude, Gemini, Open Source – through one consistent governed access layer. That’s why we love the model garden.” — Srinivasan Manoharan, Director of AI/ML Platform, PayPal.

A recurring concern we hear from enterprise leaders is the unpredictability of AI billing. When teams start scaling agents, pay-as-you-go pricing can feel like an open tab with no ceiling. That is why we optimize cost across every layer of the stack – co-designing custom TPU silicon, cluster networking, and foundation models as a single system to drive down baseline costs.

In a recent development, at the execution level, we give finance and engineering teams the right levers to innovate without risking their margins. Gemini dynamically matches every task to the most cost-effective model, handling high-volume tasks with efficient models, only escalating to frontier reasoning models for complex problem-solving. Paired with native FinOps controls – including project-level monthly spend caps, anomaly detection, and Flexible Savings Prepares – leaders get hard financial boundaries and clear visibility.

For companies processing massive volumes of data, this approach makes all the difference. At Imgix, the engineering team prioritized this architectural discipline as they scaled visual processing:.

According to recent reports, “If we're using the most expensive model every single time, that's going to be a major bill for our customers. So we use a cheaper model like Gemini Flash to figure out, ‘Does this image or video even need this AI feature?’ before routing further down the pipeline.” – Alfonso Acosta, Head of Engineering, Imgix.

Sources indicate that when organizations empower employees to build and deploy agents at scale, governance cannot be an afterthought. It must be an inherent part of the environment in which those agents operate. With Gemini, every agent is assigned a dedicated Agent Identity, ensuring that all database queries, tool actions, and state transitions generate an auditable record tied directly to authorized roles. Execution occurs inside isolated runtime sandboxes, where Agent Gateway and Model Armor automatically scrub sensitive data, block policy violations, and enforce corporate compliance in real time.

That same control plane extends to how agents interact with corporate intelligence. Rather than requiring organizations to move, replicate, or duplicate sensitive records into yet another external repository, Gemini connects directly to live enterprise systems. Agents ground their reasoning in data across BigQuery, Cloud Storage, SAP, Salesforce, S3, and Azure – inheriting existing user access controls and keeping proprietary data strictly within its original perimeter.

Governed context and centralized control are what make organization-wide agent adoption possible. UKG relied on Gemini’s security, governance, and evaluation controls to skip building that foundation from scratch:.

“The Gemini platform, it’s solving some of these key problems that we already were trying to solve — from hosting agents to securing them to the governance around them, evals to make sure they’re behaving correctly. I can just use these things out of the box and get back to creating value.” – Thomas Newton, Head of Cloud and Engineering, UKG.

Being recognized by Gartner as a Leader positioned highest in Ability to Execute reflects our commitment to meeting enterprises where they operate today. By combining frontier intelligence, universal agent orchestration across everyday tools, predictable economics, and enterprise governance, Gemini gives developers and business leaders the foundation to build with velocity and operate with confidence.

arXiv:2611.22362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals. To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, full- query differences range from 11.83 to 31.76 case points and from 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points. GPT-6-Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude-Opus-5-5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

  • Industry observers note that security teams managing thousands of instances can now prioritize patching based on actual runtime risk.
  • According to recent reports, this capability is available at no additional cost with the AWS Security Hub Essentials plan in all AWS Regions where Security Hub is available .

Sources indicate that AWS Security Hub now detects when software with a known vulnerability is actively running on your Amazon EC2 instances. Exposure findings now include a latest trait, *The EC2 instance is running software with a known vulnerability*. These findings get a higher severity rating than findings for the same vulnerability where the software isn't running. This helps your security team focus on the vulnerabilities that pose the greatest risk, without investing time and resources to investigate if the software is actually in use.

Industry observers note that security teams managing thousands of instances can now prioritize patching based on actual runtime risk. Security Hub correlates data from Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring and Amazon Inspector VM Scanner to detect running vulnerable software. It then combines this with other signals to generate exposure findings for EC2 resources that may be at risk, so you can prioritize response and remediation.

According to recent reports, this capability is available at no additional cost with the AWS Security Hub Essentials plan in all AWS Regions where Security Hub is available . To learn more, see the AWS Security Hub User Guide, the exposure definition in Remediating exposures for EC2, the AWS Security Hub product page, the GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring User Guide, and the Amazon Inspector VM Scanner User Guide. For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Model ML, a London-based personal AI platform for financial and professional services, has secured $250m in a Series B round that values the company at $1.5bn.

Recent findings suggest that general Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the investment. Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The deal lifts the total capital raised by Model ML to $350m.

The raise comes after a period of rapid expansion. Over the third quarter of 2026, annual recurring revenue at the firm increased twelvefold compared with the same period a year earlier, while daily active people rose 26-fold. Model ML plans to put the newly introduced capital towards growing its research and engineering headcount in London and New York, with the aim of advancing its product and handling larger customer rollouts. The manufacturer also opened offices this year in Paris, Madrid, Tokyo, Singapore and Dubai so it can support clients across their various locations.

Sources indicate that set up by brothers and serial founders Chaz and Arnie Englander, Model ML provides bankers, consultants and investors with an individual AI agent. The agent learns about each user’s clients, active transactions and preferred ways of working, operates on the firm’s own systems and data, runs continuously and tailors itself further with each use.

Industry observers note that rather than waiting to be prompted, it identifies what is relevant, discards distractions and acts. If a company a banker follows makes the news, the agent assesses the significance, considers the consequences and produces analysis in the firm’s house formats within minutes instead of days.

In a recent development, the platform supports a range of deployment options and is frequently installed inside clients’ own infrastructure, meaning their data stays in their environment. Client data is never used for AI model training, helping institutions protect their competitive advantage. The firm holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification and has completed a SOC 2 Type II audit.

In a recent development, model ML does not depend on a single AI vendor. It tests models against genuine financial tasks and assigns each job to whichever model offers the best balance of quality, speed and cost. An increasing proportion of its workload is handled by its own fine-tuned open-source models, which on those tasks cost 2% of what frontier models do, are typically five times quicker and equal or exceed frontier-level accuracy.

The new round builds on a $75m Series A led by FT Partners in November 2025, which also drew backing from Y Combinator, LocalGlobe, Latitude, 13Books Capital and QED Investors.

It has been revealed that model ML co-founder and CEO Chaz Englander said, “AI should do more than give you another answer or notification. It should understand your work and get things done.

“That means knowing what matters, doing the work in the background and bringing you something finished. We’re building a personal AI agent for every banker, consultant and investor, working 24/7 inside the systems their firm already trusts.”.

It has been revealed that general Atlantic managing director and global head of financial services Paul Stamas said, “Model ML is purpose-built for financial and professional services at a time when these institutions are moving quickly from AI experimentation to everyday use. We see a significant opportunity for the platform to become core to how these firms operate, with customers already trusting it with increasingly complex work.

“Model ML’s pace of customer adoption highlights that momentum is inflecting and reflects the team’s highly focused approach to innovation and execution.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that valor Capital Group led the round.
  • TheHUB’s first site, which is located within the Equinix TY15 data centre in Tokyo and is now live and bringing on exchanges, trading firms and validators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global Kiwi Labs, the developer behind digital asset colocation network TheHUB, has closed a $4m seed round as it looks to bring the equal-access trading architecture used by major traditional exchanges to digital asset markets.

It has been revealed that valor Capital Group led the round. Adderall Capital, Keyrock and Staking Facilities also invested, alongside a small number of angel backers.

TheHUB’s first site, which is located within the Equinix TY15 data centre in Tokyo and is now live and bringing on exchanges, trading firms and validators. The company will also use the money to add engineers to its team and move into further regions.

Global Kiwi Labs is targeting a structural gap in digital asset trading. Traditional exchanges have worked for decades to stop any participant from paying for a quicker route to the order book, but digital asset markets never developed an equivalent layer.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, the biggest players pay for proximity, while the rest of the market relies on slower and inconsistent links. A firm that spots a price change first can trade against participants still quoting the outdated price.

The company argues this affects more than high-frequency traders. When market makers cannot be confident their quotes will land on time, they widen spreads to offset the risk, which raises costs for every buyer and seller. Removing that uncertainty would allow tighter quoting and better pricing across the market.

TheHUB adapts four elements of traditional exchange infrastructure for digital assets. Each participant’s link to the central switch uses an identical length of fibre, calibrated to within 10 millimetres, so no firm gains a proximity edge to the matching engine.

The company mentioned that as additional exchanges and infrastructure providers join, participants gain access to a wider ecosystem without having to replicate connectivity or infrastructure spending.

Founded in 2025, TheHUB describes itself as the first colocation infrastructure purpose-built for digital markets, positioned as a transaction centre where digital assets and traditional finance meet.

Valor Capital Group partner Bruno Batavia noted, “At Valor, we look for companies building the critical infrastructure that will support the next generation of financial markets. TheHUB is developing an essential technology layer that enables digital asset markets to achieve the performance standards required by global institutional participants. Jamie and his team have demonstrated an ambitious vision combined with exceptional execution, and we’re excited to support them through this next stage of growth.”.

Global Kiwi Labs CEO Jamie Brown noted, Traditional financial markets didn’t reach today’s levels of performance through software alone. They built specialized physical infrastructure around the markets themselves. Digital asset markets are reaching the point where they need the same foundation. We’re building TheHUB so exchanges, traders, and infrastructure providers can access that foundation as a shared network rather than rebuilding it independently.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Industry observers note that note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

Industry observers note that we will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

It has been revealed that IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

In a recent development, for the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:.

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:.

Sources indicate that the IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

It has been revealed that the full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:.

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:.

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:.

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:.

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

Sources indicate that after GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it indicates that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

Sources indicate that A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

finny, a WealthTech start-up offering personalised financial advice, has reportedly secured Rs 5.3 Cr (around $560,000) through an angel round, according to a report from BW Disrupt.

The business wants to move professional advice beyond the wealthiest clients and make it available to the mass-affluent market. Its focus is on salaried households, supporting them with managing their investments, preparing for retirement and building towards lasting financial independence.

finny is a SEBI-registered adviser that charges no commission. Its service centres on the FIRE (financial independence, retire early) approach, giving customers a tailored roadmap with practical steps. Customers can work out the age at which they could stop depending on a salary, along with the size of the fund needed, based on their goals and spending. A FIRE score reviews their finances across three areas: whether savings are on track, whether investments are growing efficiently, and how well a portfolio could cope with personal or market shocks.

Prospective clients can book a free 45-minute one-to-one session with a SEBI-registered adviser to spot weaknesses in their finances and agree next steps. The firm also provides a one-off portfolio reset covering investment clean-up, tax harvesting and cash flow guidance. This can be followed by an ongoing personal CFO strategy, under which an adviser monitors investments and taxes throughout the year.

Director, Product Management, Cloud Networking.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As AI changes how businesses build and run applications, more enterprises are spreading their models, data and applications across multiple clouds. To make that work, they need fast, private connections between those environments. Historically, connecting multiple clouds has meant ordering physical connections from each provider, setting up networking on both sides, and coordinating across multiple teams. That process could take weeks or even months.

According to recent reports, we wanted to make that much simpler. Today, we're extending partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect to Microsoft Azure, now available in preview. The service is jointly supported by Google Cloud and Microsoft, and gives you a private, high-bandwidth connection between your Google Cloud and Azure environments that’s set up programmatically in minutes, with no physical infrastructure to manage.

"Google Cloud partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect simplifies multi-cloud networking with a direct cloud-native approach. By removing traditional infrastructure complexity, it provides a reliable, scalable foundation for connecting workloads across different cloud environments." - Ralf Huebenthal, Global Head of IT & Digital Platforms, Nestlé.

In a recent development, “Walmart runs a seamless platform across multiple cloud providers to accelerate innovations. We partner with Google Cloud to leverage their global network for hybrid and multicloud networking. With Cross-Cloud Interconnect, we were able to simplify connectivity between cloud providers, shorten time to production, and reduce overall costs.” - Gerald Bothello, Group Director of Software Engineering, Walmart.

In a recent development, on-demand connectivity in minutes, not weeks. Set up your connection from the Google Cloud console or API, pick the bandwidth you need, and both clouds handle the rest — no hardware to order, no manual network configuration, and no back and forth between providers.

According to recent reports, built-in reliability. Your connection runs across physically separate locations for redundancy. Google Cloud and Azure jointly monitor the connection and handle maintenance and recovery for you.

Private and secure. Your traffic stays off the public internet, and is automatically encrypted between the Google Cloud and Azure edge routers, with no customer configuration required.

Recent findings suggest that predictable pricing. You pay a fixed price for the connection's bandwidth, so your Google Cloud costs are easy to strategy and manage.

"Customers are building applications, data platforms and AI across more than one cloud, and they want the network between those clouds to just work. Azure Multicloud Interconnect with Google Cloud gives customers a private, managed path between Azure and Google Cloud, and we're excited to work with Google Cloud to bring it to customers in public preview." - Sudha Mahajan, Partner, Product Management, Azure Networking, Microsoft.

Our Cross-Cloud Interconnect ecosystem continues to expand:.

Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for Microsoft Azure is available in preview today in us-east4 (N. Virginia), us-west2 (Los Angeles), and europe-west3 (Frankfurt), alongside the generally available AWS and OCI offerings. We'll add more regions as the Azure offering moves to general availability.

Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for last mile with Lumen is available in preview, for customers connecting their private clouds, on-premises sites, and neocloud environments to Google Cloud.

Recent findings suggest that partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect is built on an open specification for network interoperability. Google Cloud collaborated with AWS and published it last year, and any provider can adopt it.

To learn more, visit the partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect documentation, read Microsoft's announcement, or contact your Google Cloud account team.

NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • In a recent development, we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

In a recent development, we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

Industry observers note that modernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

According to recent reports, neoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

According to recent reports, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

Sources indicate that we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

According to recent reports, one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

In a recent development, † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

It has been revealed that we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Customers can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding fresh documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

Sources indicate that neoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers presently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Sources indicate that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

Recent findings suggest that neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Manufacturer for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22338v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An key challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AWS Network Firewall attached to AWS Transit Gateway now allows you to use context-aware rules in your firewall policy.
  • Context-aware rules match traffic using VPCs, subnets, security groups, and Transit Gateway attachment identifiers, collectively known as context identifiers.
  • Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

It has been revealed that AWS Network Firewall attached to AWS Transit Gateway now allows you to use context-aware rules in your firewall policy. Network Firewall is a managed firewall and intrusion prevention service that inspects and filters traffic across your virtual private clouds (VPCs). With context-aware rules, you write rules that reference context from VPC resources instead of IP addresses. This makes it easier to apply consistent security controls as your organization grows. Existing rules automatically cover latest workloads, so you don't need to update rules manually.

Context-aware rules match traffic using VPCs, subnets, security groups, and Transit Gateway attachment identifiers, collectively known as context identifiers. You can reference context identifiers in a rule's source for any protocol, and in its destination for TCP-based protocols such as HTTP, TLS, and SSH. Flow and alert logs include context identifiers, so you can investigate activity based on context.

Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. For a full list of supported Regions, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page.

To learn more, see the AWS Network Firewall product page and documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • nCino, the agentic AI banking platform, has made its Loan Marketplace for participations generally available to US financial institutions.
  • Banks and credit unions that already use nCino Portfolio Analytics can access the fresh product straight away within their existing nCino instance.
  • The marketplace extends the functionality of Portfolio Analytics, a tool more than 1,000 financial institutions at the moment rely on for loan-level performance insight, individualised forward-looking risk modelling, balance sheet management and compliance with the Current Expected Credit Losses standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

nCino, the agentic AI banking platform, has made its Loan Marketplace for participations generally available to US financial institutions.

Banks and credit unions that already use nCino Portfolio Analytics can access the fresh product straight away within their existing nCino instance.

The marketplace extends the functionality of Portfolio Analytics, a tool more than 1,000 financial institutions at the moment rely on for loan-level performance insight, individualised forward-looking risk modelling, balance sheet management and compliance with the Current Expected Credit Losses standard.

Since each institution’s loan information is already standardised within its Portfolio Analytics environment, there is no need to recreate a loan tape in a spreadsheet or separate application. Sellers can assemble pools directly from their own portfolio data, while prospective buyers can examine a pool’s analytics, along with risk and performance details for each individual loan, before submitting an offer.

The result is a single destination where institutions can sell, purchase and oversee participations, covering everything from pre-commitment pool analysis to post-closing remittance calculation and validation.

On the selling side, the platform offers guided pool building based on eligibility criteria and retention rules set by the seller. It also provides pool analytics spanning concentration, credit risk, gross yield and pricing sensitivity, as well as role-based approval controls that record who created and who signed off each listing.

Buyers, meanwhile, can review pools using loan-level risk and performance analytics, export a list of the loans involved and work through a due diligence process in which expressions of interest, letters of intent and supporting documentation are exchanged inside the marketplace.

According to recent reports, for ongoing management, a guided monthly reconciliation highlights any discrepancies and demands seller review and approval before funds are released. People also gain a consistent view of performance, delinquency, charge-offs, maturity and concentration for pools traded via the marketplace, as well as for sold pools brought in from other sources.

Sources indicate that participations have become an vital lever for balance sheet management, with institutions often mapping out purchases and sales months in advance to hit portfolio goals such as loan-to-share or loan-to-deposit ratios when fresh lending falls short. They also help firms tackle concentration risk by broadening their portfolios beyond the loans they can originate themselves. At 31 October 2026, nCino’s Portfolio Analytics customers held over $21bn in loan participations and trade substantial volumes annually. However, the supporting tools have lagged behind.

According to nCino, brokers, listing boards and existing participation marketplaces typically do not hold the underlying portfolio data. As a result, buyers frequently price pools without proper visibility into the loans they contain, and post-sale servicing often depends on spreadsheets sent by email in varying formats. By linking the marketplace to each institution’s own data in Portfolio Analytics, nCino aims to introduce more transparency, automation and efficiency to a market historically driven by personal contacts, phone calls and spreadsheets.

It has been revealed that nCino serves more than 2,700 customers globally, ranging from community banks, credit unions and independent mortgage banks to some of the world’s largest financial organisations. Its agentic platform is designed specifically for financial services and other regulated sectors, pairing AI agents with human staff to help institutions remove inefficiencies, improve decision-making and achieve better results for their customers.

According to recent reports, nCino CEO Sean Desmond said, “Participation trading keeps growing across the industry. EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (281 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Recent findings suggest that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • Recent findings suggest that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Recent findings suggest that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

Recent findings suggest that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

It has been revealed that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

Industry observers note that that same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

Sources indicate that there's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

Sources indicate that this is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

Sources indicate that gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

Industry observers note that this is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Recent findings suggest that background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

Sources indicate that there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

Industry observers note that AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

Sources indicate that the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

Industry observers note that A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

Recent findings suggest that zeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

According to recent reports, this isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

In a recent development, every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node demonstrates up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

In a recent development, now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

According to recent reports, AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

Sources indicate that bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

In a recent development, really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

According to recent reports, analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?
